lesson.title: Measuring the Mismatch: The Chi-Square Statistic
lesson.summary: The chi-square statistic sums (observed minus expected) squared over expected across all categories, producing a single non-negative number that measures how far observed counts are from what a hypothesis predicts.
lesson.body:
The chi-square statistic is defined as the sum, across every category, of (observed minus expected) squared, divided by expected: chi-square equals the sum of (O minus E) squared over E. Each piece of that formula earns its place. The raw difference, O minus E, measures how far off a single category's observed count is from what was expected there. Squaring that difference makes every category's contribution positive, so an over-count in one category cannot cancel out an under-count in another when everything is added together, and it penalizes larger gaps more than proportionally more than smaller ones. Dividing by E rescales the squared gap relative to how big that category was expected to be in the first place, so a gap of 5 counts matters far more when only 10 counts were expected there than when 1000 were expected.

This formula also explains why the statistic can never be negative, matching what was said about the chi-square distribution itself: every single term being summed is a square divided by a positive number, so no term can be negative, and a sum of non-negative terms is non-negative. A chi-square statistic near 0 means the observed counts matched the expected counts almost perfectly. A large chi-square statistic means at least one category, and often several, deviated substantially from what was expected.

Here is a full worked example. A die is rolled 60 times to check whether it is fair. If the die is fair, each of the 6 faces is expected to come up 60 divided by 6, or 10 times. Suppose the actual observed counts are: face 1, 8 times; face 2, 11 times; face 3, 7 times; face 4, 14 times; face 5, 12 times; face 6, 8 times (these do add to 60, a useful check). Computing each category's contribution: (8 minus 10) squared divided by 10 equals 4 divided by 10, or 0.4. (11 minus 10) squared divided by 10 equals 1 divided by 10, or 0.1. (7 minus 10) squared divided by 10 equals 9 divided by 10, or 0.9. (14 minus 10) squared divided by 10 equals 16 divided by 10, or 1.6. (12 minus 10) squared divided by 10 equals 4 divided by 10, or 0.4. (8 minus 10) squared divided by 10 equals 4 divided by 10, or 0.4. Adding these six contributions: 0.4 plus 0.1 plus 0.9 plus 1.6 plus 0.4 plus 0.4 equals 3.8. So the chi-square statistic here is 3.8.

A bigger chi-square statistic signals observed data farther from what was expected under whatever hypothesis generated the expected counts. Whether 3.8 counts as far enough to be convincing depends on comparing it to the right chi-square distribution, using its degrees of freedom as a reference, exactly what the goodness-of-fit test, next, uses this statistic to do.
